evidence.text: The page interprets the oracle form of 老 as a bent, long-haired person holding a staff, and identifies the oracle staff element as 丨. It says bronze forms render the staff in 匕 shape, sometimes miswritten 止; upper parts vary from the Spring and Autumn period onward, and one form may use 由 as a phonetic element, though the page does not establish this as the graph’s original formation. It reports an oracle-bone place-name use, bronze uses for an elder, ‘old’, senior ministers, and 老 written for 考 ‘father’, plus Warring States examples. These reported examples do not by themselves establish a semantic chronology.
evidence.title: 漢語甲骨部件分析: 老

evidence.source: ShuoWen.org, 說文解字 and 段玉裁注
evidence.text: The Eastern Han Shuowen account glosses 老 as 考, defines a person aged seventy as 老, and analyzes its form as 人、毛、匕, explaining it through whitening hair. Duan Yucai records debate about 老 and 考 and the 轉注 account; he suggests the seal form may derive from 毛匕, with 人 not a separate element. This is historical lexicographic interpretation, not direct evidence of the oracle form’s origin.
evidence.title: 說文解字「老」

evidence.text: The file page identifies 老-oracle.svg as a vector depiction of 老 in Shang oracle-script style, gives j19923 and Hanziyuan as the specific image reference, and marks the representation public domain. This is a modern digital vector redraw, not a photograph or scan of an ancient artifact.

gaps: The earliest cited oracle instance on the CUHK page is a place-name occurrence; its connection, if any, to the lexical meaning ‘old’ is not established, and no absolute date for that specific inscription was recovered.

CUHK reports later bronze lexical uses and Warring States examples, but original artifacts and transmitted-text editions were not separately inspected here; the examples do not define the order or semantic links among the senses.

The exact sequence of graphic change is only partly documented. The character-specific account supports variation in the staff form and later upper-part variation, but does not establish when or why a particular apparent miswriting arose beyond its description as 訛寫.

The ShuoWen component analysis and Duan Yucai’s alternative reading are later analyses; neither independently confirms the oracle graph’s formation. No sound component is established for the original graph; CUHK only says one later variant may have a phonetic role.
Commons provides a reusable modern redraw in oracle style, not an ancient artifact image. No eligible exact Xiaoxuetang 老 glyph candidate or official rights notice was verified.

No complete source reuse terms for CUHK or the online Shuowen text were verified; no local extracts are recommended. The local Baxter–Sagart and Unihan rows supplied in the dossier were not independently rechecked or externally validated in this web pass.
